title: Client expectations, value and authenticity claims
referencesAtStart: Official references for this lesson: OAIC, Privacy for small business (published 10 March 2023, per page metadata).
audience: Furniture restorers and staff who talk with clients about restoration work, results and value.
learningOutcomes: Set out what restoration will and will not change, and put the limits in writing.
Avoid claims of age, value, authenticity or lead-free and asbestos-free status that the evidence does not support.
Handle client photos and item details with the business's privacy approach.

instruction.heading: Set expectations early
instruction.body: Restoration shows the piece's history and its wear. It does not return the piece to new. Explain what will change, what will stay, and what cannot be guaranteed, such as an exact colour match, full removal of every mark, or a fixed cure outcome. Show a test piece or sample where you can, and put the main limits in writing before work starts.

instruction.heading: Age, value and authenticity
instruction.body: Do not describe a piece as an antique, original, heritage or valuable unless the client has documentation, or a qualified appraiser has confirmed it. Do not say that a repair will raise the piece's value. Describe what the work does to the piece. Where the client asks about age or value, suggest a qualified appraiser and record the conversation.

instruction.heading: Lead, asbestos and health statements
instruction.body: Do not tell a client that an item is lead-free or asbestos-free without a result that supports the statement. Do not describe a finish as safe for children or pets without the product's label and SDS. If screening found a positive or unknown result, tell the client plainly, record the advice given, and refer the material as “Screen for lead and asbestos: test, stop and refer” sets out. Share results as results. Share the regulator's or specialist's advice with them as well.

instruction.heading: Privacy and complaints
instruction.body: Store photographs and item details securely. Ask for the client's permission before sharing photographs of their home, belongings or the piece, including on social media. Whether the Privacy Act binds the business depends on turnover and activity: businesses with turnover at or under $3 million are generally outside it unless an exception applies. Use the approved wording in {{business:customers.communication_policy}}. If a client complains, record the complaint, acknowledge it, and escalate it as {{business:customers.complaint_escalation}} sets out.

procedure: Explain what the work will and will not change, and show a test piece or sample where possible.
Confirm the expectations and limits in writing before work starts.
Keep every claim to what the work and the results support.
Refer any age, value or authenticity question to a qualified appraiser, and record the conversation.
Get permission before sharing photographs, and store item details securely.
Record any complaint, acknowledge it, and escalate it as the policy sets out.

workedExamples.situation: A client says a walnut desk is an antique and asks, 'Will this add a lot to its value?'
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not confirm the age or the value. Describe what the restoration will do to the desk, and suggest a qualified appraiser for questions about age and value. Record the conversation and what was said. Do not give a figure to keep the client happy.

equipmentAndPpe: Test piece or finish sample for showing the client
Secure storage for photographs and item records

commonErrors.prevention: Show the test piece, and say the match depends on the timber and the light.

commonErrors.error: Calling a piece an antique without documentation.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the piece as it is, and refer age questions to a qualified appraiser.

commonErrors.error: Telling a client a finish is lead-free without a test.
commonErrors.prevention: Say no result exists, and arrange screening as “Screen for lead and asbestos: test, stop and refer” sets out.

commonErrors.error: Sharing photographs of a client's home without permission.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask for permission and record it before any photo is shared.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Statements about health, safety or value must match the test results, the product's SDS and label, and any documentation.
Lead and asbestos results are shared with the client as factual results, with the regulator's or specialist's advice. A result is not a clearance unless it says so.

qualityStandard: The client has agreed the expectations and limits in writing.
No quote, invoice or marketing text makes a claim the evidence does not support.
Photographs are shared only with permission.
documentationEvidence: Expectations and limits note, with client sign-off
Record of any age, value or screening conversation
Complaint record and escalation, where relevant
summary: Restoration shows history and wear. It does not return a piece to new.
Do not claim age, value, authenticity or lead-free and asbestos-free status without evidence.
Get permission before sharing photographs, and record complaints.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks whether a chair is an antique that will be worth more after repair. What is the best response?
options: Yes, it will double in value once the repair is finished and the finish is restored
Give a rough figure to keep the client happy and make the call feel friendly and warm
Describe what the work does, and suggest a qualified appraiser for questions of age and value

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks whether the finish is lead-free, and no test has been done. What should the restorer say?
options: No result exists, so the restorer cannot say; arrange screening
Yes, it is lead-free, since the finish looks modern and clean
Lead does not occur in furniture of this type and age at all

knowledgeChecks.question: Before a photo of a client's home is shared on social media, what is required?
options: Nothing, if the photo is good and shows the finished work clearly
The client's permission, handled under the business's privacy approach
The client's signature on the invoice, which covers all photos
